newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mineral wealth lures investors to troubled Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Mineral wealth lures investors to troubled Zaire.

text.p: Zaire may be in political chaos and battling a burgeoning rebel campaign but its huge mineral wealth is luring some investors hoping for a major revival of the mining industry, analysts said on Tuesday.

With Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko's rule of the vast Central African country under threat from the Rwandan-backed rebels fears have been expressed that Zaire could break up, sparking more violence and creating a refugee crisis.
Nonetheless, several foreign mining companies have set up shop in Zaire, hoping to unlock the abundant untapped reserves of copper, cobalt, diamonds and gold.
"Overall, I am very positive that we are going to see a significant recovery in the Zairean mining industry," Johannesburg-based investment analyst John Clemmow said.

Last week, Zaire state-owned copper company Gecamines signed its first major joint venture with a foreign company which the major backer -- Swiss-based financier Adolf Lundin -- described as "the rebirth of Zaire's mining industry".

Lundin's Groupe Lundin, together with Canadian exploration company Consolidated Eurocan Ventures, won the right to explore and possibly mine the Tenke Fungurume copper and cobalt ore body in the southern Shaba province.
Tenke Fungurume is one of the largest such resources in the world and boasts high grades of copper, easily accessible.
Consolidated Eurocan technical director Brian Spratley told a Metal Bulletin mining and metals conference on Tuesday the company hoped to begin production by 2000.
The company, soon to be renamed Tenke Mining Corp, sees a two-year feasibility study at Tenke Fungurame ending in 1998 and first production beginning in 2000.
It will aim to produce around 100,000 tonnes of copper and 8,500 tonnes of cobalt by 2002, lifting output to 400,000 tonnes of copper and 17,000 tonnes of cobalt in 2012, Spratley said.
"Technical risks are low and mining is seen as a means to economic recovery for the country," he added.
Zaire's copper production dropped from 500,000 tonnes in 1978 to around 30,000 tonnes in 1995 reflecting the decline of the country's economy.
Despite the country's current problems, the mining revival would not be easily stopped, Clemmow said.
"Irrespective of what happens in Zaire, Shaba is going to be developed. It is going to go through, the political shenanigans will have no effect," Clemmow said.

Clemmow and other analysts said the Tenke Fungurume project alone would not be the salvation of Zaire's mining industry but pointed out that several other projects were under investigation by major mining companies, including South Africa's giant Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd.
Anglo has tendered to develop the Kolwezi tailings project, which aims to produce around 6,000 tonnes of cobalt a year from tailings left over from copper mining.

Other foreign companies who have expressed interest in Zaire's mineral wealth include Gencor Ltd and Iscor Ltd, Broken Hill Proprietary Ltd (BHP), Barrick Gold Corp and several junior mining companies.
South African mining giant De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd also maintains several diamond buying offices in Zaire.

"What seems to happen is that once one person takes the plunge into a country it brings with it a flood of other things. You have seen that in West Africa with the gold mining industry," said metals analyst Stephen Briggs of stockbrokers E.W Balderson.
But Briggs said it would take time to develop the long-neglected Zairean mining industry.
"This (Tenke Fungurume) could be one of the catalysts to revive things but I don't think it's going to be tomorrow".
